title: Colombia earthquake live updates: more than 100 dead and buildings collapsed after 7.4-magnitude quake
summary: More than a dozen buildings collapsed in aftermath of earthquake, which has also prompted evacuations
body: The Colombia earthquake has left many people trapped under the debris of damaged buildings as their loved ones and rescue workers search through the rubble. Search teams and civilians picked through the remains of destroyed buildings in the country’s third-largest city, Cali, passing large pieces of concrete and other rubble down a long line of volunteers. “Our building has basically been left in ruins, and the building next to ours? Completely collapsed,” said Álvaro López, who cradled his dog as he watched the search. The desperate scene recalled the searches still ongoing in neighbouring Venezuela weeks after that country was devastated by back-to-back quakes in June, the Associated Press reports. Besides Cali, the quake-ravaged cities across western Colombia including Pereira, Quibdo and Manizales and was felt in neighboring Ecuador and Panama. At least 111 have died and 87 people injured after dozens of buildings collapsed following a 7.4 magnitude earthquake that struck western Colombia on Monday morning – the largest to hit the country so far this century. After declaring a state of national disaster, Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said in an address to the nation that his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” he said after around 1,600 buildings had been damaged, including at least 61 that completely collapsed. The president declared an emergency to expedite funding for the quake recovery while saying he would visit the disaster zone. “We aren’t going to leave people alone. They are in our hearts and we are going to tend to people with our full determination,” he said. The quake hit the remote Chocó region around 7.30am local time on Monday morning and was felt as far as the capital Bogotá (250 miles away), as well as neighbouring countries Ecuador, Venezuela and Panama. The epicentre was in San Jose Del Palmar, a community of about 4,800 people, and the initial quake was followed by two 2.8 and 4.8 magnitude aftershocks. Local officials confirmed deaths across several regions, including the coffee region of Risaralda and in Valle del Cauca, while rescue teams race to free people trapped under debris of collapsed buildings. Among the worst-hit areas was the city of Pereira, where at least 40 people have been killed, according to the mayor. In the department of Chocó, at least 12 people were killed, according to the local governor there, and at least 27 deaths have been reported in the neighbouring Valle del Cauca department, including at least three children and including 15 people in Cali, Colombia’s third-largest city. The United States and countries across Europe and Latin America offered support. The Trump administration is “closely monitoring” the earthquake, US secretary of state Marco Rubio said earlier, adding that Washington “stands ready to support” the people and the pro-Trump government. Other countries including Ecuador, France, Mexico and Brazil also offered support. It all comes less than two months after two earthquakes devastated parts of Venezuela, killing more than 6,100 people. The mayor of Pereira has declared a state of public emergency and manifest urgency, along with a curfew that will be in effect from 6pm on Monday until 5am Tuesday in the following areas: Centro, Comuna Universidad, and SubCentro de la Comuna Cuba. A car-free day measure will also start at 4pm on Monday and all day on Tuesday. Classes in educational institutions are also suspended. “As mayor of Pereira, I must appeal to the solidarity of all Pereirans to go home because we need traffic to flow for emergency response agencies. We need to address this emergency. That is why, starting at this moment, I declare the Exceptional State of Curfew. Starting at this moment and indefinitely, classes are suspended in all educational institutions,” said Mauricio Salazar. In the city, located in the heart of the coffee-producing mountains of Colombia and around 35 miles from the earthquake’s epicentre, 40 people have been reported dead. According to the mayor’s update, 65 buildings collapsed in the metropolitan area, and people are assumed trapped in 15 of them. Several clinics were forced to close due either to demand on services or infrastructure risks, while Matecaña airport “suffered damage to its facilities, with several people deceased”. Several people are also trapped in gondolas in Megacable, and the mayor said the rescue process for them would begin soon, but for the time being “their lives are not in danger at this moment” and “priority is being given to collapsed buildings”. Colombia’s vice-president, José Manuel Restrepo Abondano, posted on X: Mr. President, I heed your instruction. We already have the support of our international allies who have responded with solidarity and commitment. We will not rest until that aid reaches every family that needs it and contributes to the recovery of the affected territories. Today the world extends a hand to #Colombia, and we will stand by every community struck by this tragedy, working tirelessly to help it move forward. As we reported earlier, world leaders including the US and EU have sent messages of solidarity and offered support to Colombia. Ecuador’s president Daniel Noboa Azin also offered 47 rescuers, specialized dogs, and equipment with autonomy to operate for 7 days. “We are ready to mobilize whenever you require,” he wrote on X. Mexico’s president Claudia Sheinbaum also wrote: “Of course, all the support that the people of Colombia may require; we’ll be there.” Brazil’s Lula also expressed his solidarity, writing on X: “Brazil remains at Colombia’s disposal to provide the necessary support.” Nayib Bukele, president of El Salvador, said he was in communication with Colombian officials and was “ready to provide immediate support with our rescue teams, medical personnel, paramedics, supplies, or any other assistance that our Colombian brothers and sisters deem necessary”. In Europe, French president Emmanuel Macron said: “I extend, on behalf of France, my most sincere thoughts to the Colombian people. I think of the victims, their families, the injured, and all those who have been affected by this disaster. Our solidarity also goes to the rescue teams and all those who are working, with courage, to assist the affected populations. In this ordeal, Colombia can count on our friendship and our support.” Spanish prime minister Pedro Sánchez also offered “affection and solidarity with the Colombian people” and said Spain “stands with Colombia” at this difficult time. Italian PM Giorgia Meloni said she was “anxiously” following updates on the earthquake. “In these difficult hours, Italy stands in solidarity with the Colombian people, the affected families, and all those engaged in rescue and assistance operations,” she said. And Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine stands in “full support” and offered his condolences to those who have lost loved ones. “We call on everyone around the world who can support the affected people and countries right now to step up and help,” he wrote on X. Colombian pop star Shakira has said her heart is with “everyone who felt this earthquake today”. “In times like these, we Colombians know how to come together and support one another,” she wrote on X. “All my strength and love for my homeland. Let’s embrace tightly and stay tuned to the instructions so we can help as soon as possible.” European Commission president Ursula von der Leyen said on Monday that the European Union was “ready to provide more support” to Colombia. “Tonight, Europe’s heart is with the people of Colombia after the terrible earthquake in the Choco region. We have already mobilised Copernicus, our satellite service, to help with rescue operations,” she wrote on social media. Santiago Velázquez, an industrial advisor, was driving to his son’s school in the suburbs between Pereira and Cartago, in Colombia’s Risaralda province, when the quake hit. All the cars had to stop because they were being thrown around as the earth shook, Velázquez said. He was already outside when it happened. “But people were falling and being struck by things as they tried to get out of their buildings,” he said. Traffic is totally stuck at the moment, so Velázquez is getting a motorbike into the centre to try and help friends and family. He knows of one landslide that carried away a few houses, and he had heard reports of some five-storey buildings in the suburbs that are “totally cracked”. Some areas were without water, light or gas. A “disaster”, Velázquez said. In an address to the nation around midday (local time), president de la Espriella said his government had deployed all of its capabilities “to protect lives, assist affected ‌communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed”. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble,” he said. The 7.4 magnitude quake struck at a depth ⁠of 107 km (66 miles) in Choco, a sparsely populated province on Colombia’s Pacific coast, but was felt in major cities nationwide. Colombia’s new president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said the death toll from the earthquake has now reached 111, Reuters is reporting. At least 87 were injured and 61 buildings collapsed, he said, noting the rescue of survivors was his priority. The death toll continues to climb after a powerful earthquake hit western Colombia on Monday. At least 82 people have been confirmed dead, Reuters is reporting. The province of Risaralda, in Colombia’s coffee-growing region, has suffered the highest toll so far, with governor Juan Diego Patino reporting 42 fatalities. Dozens of injuries and heavy damage to buildings were also reported in Choco, the province closest to the epicentre of the 7.4 magnitude quake. title: Trump signs executive order to split measles, mumps and rubella vaccine into separate shots in sweeping change – live
summary: He added that his administration would no longer recommend hepatitis b, Covid-19 and influenza shots for children
body: Also asking Max Miller to step aside are members of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, one of whom called the allegations against the congressmember “horrific” and “credible.” “The horrific allegations levied against Max Miller, who has a lengthy record of alleged domestic violence, are credible and cannot be ignored,” said DCCC spokesperson Riya Vashi. “Rather than step aside, Miller has chosen to cling to power and put his family and his constituents through a public spectacle of his own making,” Vashi added. “Let’s be clear: this is the same playbook Max Miller has run before — deny, deflect, and drag his accusers through the mud.” The Trump administration has extended for 90 days ⁠a waiver allowing foreign-flagged ships carrying oil and gas to travel between US ports, White House spokesperson Taylor Rogers said in a post on social media. The waiver extension, which will take effect on 17 August, applies to the Jones Act, a law passed in 1920 that requires shipping between ports in the US to be conducted under US ships. Rogers said the extension was granted to “ensure our military and key industries maintain uninterrupted access to critical resources”. “Data shows the waiver has driven a significant increase in domestic deliveries of essential products such as gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel,” Rogers wrote. New limits were imposed after shipbuilders and members in Congress argued the policy was undermining the domestic maritime ⁠industry. Now, the waiver will only apply to cargo that are sources of energy and commodities related to agriculture, per the AP. The waiver comes as the strait of Hormuz, a primary waterway for shipping oil and natural gas, remains effectively closed because of the war. Ironworker Brian Poindexter, a Democrat challenging the embattled congressman Max Miller in Ohio, said that his opponent “should be in prison, not in Congress” if the allegations of domestic abuse are true. “It’s unfortunate that Miller has chosen to keep putting his ex-wife and her family through this nightmare in the public spotlight,” Poindexter said in a statement. “But let me be perfectly clear. I got into this campaign to fight for my neighbors and for working people across this district,” he added. “That continues to be my north star. Our campaign’s doors are wide open to anyone - Democrat, Republican, or anything in between - who believes their representative should serve with honor and work for Ohioans, not for special interests and not for themselves. In November, we will win this race, and the people of the 7th District will finally have a representative who fights for them.” Speaking to reporters earlier, Donald Trump said that the US retains the full capability to escalate actions against Iran if it chooses to do so. “We have certainly that ability if we want to do that,” Trump said. “You’ll find out.” Echoing remarks he wrote in a Truth Social post, Trump said Iran should pay for “the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period” instead of the US paying for the damage caused by the bombardment in Iran over the past five months. “They ask for money for the damage that we’ve done. I said: ‘that’s a good idea. Well, we’re going to ask for money for the damage they’ve done over a 50-year period’,” he said. “If there’s damages to be paid, I think Iran should pay those damages.” Donald Trump signed an executive order today that will involve splitting up the highly effective measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three single shots. The president also announced an overhaul to the childhood immunization schedule, scrapping recommendations for the hepatitis b, Covid-19 and influenza vaccines. He also suggested that the number of inoculations is linked to the rate of autism in the US, despite no proven link between the two. Todd Blanche was officially sworn in as the new attorney general. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was narrowly confirmed in the role by the Senate. Every Democrat rejected Blanche’s nomination. Lawyers for David Hearn, the Olympian who was arrested for alleged property destruction of the reflecting pool before his charges were dropped, said that the Trump administration is “continuing to attack an innocent man”. This comes after Donald Trump said that Hearn was still guilty on Truth Social this weekend, despite the justice department dismissing all charges against him, and citing the “botched” renovation of the pool as the reason for the peeling lining. Trump also said today that he is “demanding compensation from Iran” in future talks. This comes after Tehran tied compensation for the damage caused by the war launched by the US and Israel at the end of February to the reopening of the strategic strait of Hormuz. Trump said the matter of compensation “was never mentioned in any of our negotiations or meetings”, but Tehran has been demanding war damages from Washington since the early weeks of the war. Later he said that Iran should be responsible for “the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza”. The Trump administration has repeatedly pointed to Europe as a model – arguing that EU countries do not require childhood vaccinations. In reality, 12 EU nations mandate certain vaccines for children. France, Germany, Italy, Hungary, Croatia, Bulgaria, Czechia, Latvia, Poland, Slovakia and Slovenia all require the measles vaccination for infants, for example. As my colleague Melody Schreiber notes, while Trump’s latest order requires clinicians to offer three separate shots to protect against measles, mumps and rubella, there are actually no separately licensed vaccines for the diseases, and the licensing process takes years. A reminder that the changes recommended to the childhood vaccine schedule were first suggested by the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP) earlier this year. However, they were blocked by a federal judge. We can expect that these latest attempts overhaul the immunization schedule will be met by further legal challenges. In the Oval Office, Donald Trump has signed an executive order – that we flagged earlier – which would split up the measles, mumps and rubella vaccines. “You should have five separate visits for vaccines rather than giving them all in the same day,” the president said. He added that his administration would no longer recommend hepatitis b, Covid-19 and influenza shots for children. “Decades ago, children received only a small fraction of the vaccines required today. In those times, people were much healthy, and of course, the high rates of autism now observed did not exist. So there’s a reason for such epidemic rates of autism, and we’re going to bring it back to much closer to where it was,” Trump said, despite the fact that there is no proven link between inoculations and an increased risk of autism. Earlier, we reported that Trump is “demanding compensation from Iran”, tied compensation for the damage caused by the war launched by the US and Israel. In a follow-up post on Truth Social, the president said that Tehran should be responsible for “the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza”. In a closed-press ceremony, Todd Blanche was officially sworn in as the new attorney general. In a video posted to social media, press secretary Karoline Leavitt filmed Blanche taking the oath of office while Donald Trump stood beside him in the Oval Office. Blanche has been serving as acting attorney general since April. The Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation in the role, with the Republican-led upper chamber voting 50-49 in the early hours of Saturday morning. Every Democrat rejected his nomination. Donald Trump is set to sign an executive order today that will involve splitting up the highly effective measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine into three single shots. Last year, the advisory committee on immunization practices (ACIP), which health secretary Robert F Kennedy Jr overhauled and replaced with several vaccine-skeptics, voted to change US vaccine policy and recommend single vaccines to protect against measles, mumps, rubella and chickenpox, instead of a single shot that can protect against all four diseases. Kirk Milhoan, the ACIP chair, telegraphed earlier this year that he expects the US childhood vaccine schedule to undergo changes. ACIP may “not necessarily” change the recommendations for all vaccines to become optional, but the committee is “reevaluating all of the vaccine products including risks and benefits”, Milhoan told the New York Times in January. Many public health experts have warned that splitting up shots could increase the likelihood of missed visits and reduced immunization. 2026 has already seen the highest number of measles cases throughout the US in 35 years, according to data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). Meanwhile, in Charleston, South Carolina, defense secretary Pete Hegseth unveiled that the area’s main airbase has now been renamed in honor of the late Republican senator Lindsey Graham. “It now falls to us to continue Senator Graham’s work, of building up our military, the hard work of defending this nation,” Hegseth said, while unveiling Joint Base Lindsey Graham. The late lawmaker served for three decades in the US military, retiring with the rank of colonel. Todd Blanche has arrived at the White House for his swearing-in ceremony. The event is currently closed to the press, but we’ll let you know if anything changes. Joe Gruters, the Republican National Committee (RNC) chair, avoided calling on Max Miller – the embattled Ohio congressman facing a wave of domestic abuse allegations and pressure to resign – to end his re-election bid. “I always tell people that there’s not many things worse than divorce,” Gruters said in an interview with NewsNation. “Nobody’s a winner.” A reminder that Miller’s ex-wife, Emily Moreno, is the daughter of Ohio Senator Bernie…

title: Nearly 30 pine trees intentionally poisoned in Lake Tahoe’s Nevada side
summary: Incidents of damaged trees at Burnt Cedar beach have been reported since 2022 and seem to be linked, officials say
body: Pine trees near Lake Tahoe are being poisoned in what authorities believe are a series of interconnected incidents in the popular tourist community on border of Nevada and California. The incidents have damaged nearly 30 trees, some reportedly more than a century old, and caused hundreds of thousands of dollars in losses. Officials in Nevada said 28 trees were poisoned at Burnt Cedar beach, a restricted-access beach located on the north-east shore of Lake Tahoe. Six trees were also damaged in 2022, another six in 2024, and 16 more were discovered this year. In a statement released on Thursday, authorities said that the incidents appear to be connected, causing an estimated $300,000 in losses. No suspect has been identified or arrested. “We take these crimes very seriously and will utilize every available resource to identify and apprehend the person or persons responsible,” said the office of Darin Balaam, the Washoe county sheriff, in a statement. “The destruction of mature trees in the Tahoe Basin and the environmental damage caused by these deliberate acts are unacceptable.” The most recent incidents were reported in late July and early August. On 24 July, deputies responded to the beach after a strong odor was detected near a large pine tree. Soil samples collected from the area had an odor consistent with other incidents related to the pine trees at the property, according to the county sheriff’s office. Officials returned on 2 August after more trees were found with a substance around their bases. Authorities believe the most recent incident occurred sometime between 11.30am on 1 August and 5am on 2 August. Authorities are still investigating the substance used to poison the trees in the residents-only beach in Incline Village. Investigators have collected soil samples for testing to determine which substance was used and whether the same substance was involved in each incident. In some instances, officials found holes had been drilled near the roots of the pines in Incline Village. Authorities said that, based on the estimated amount of damage, the person or people responsible could face felony-level charges. Incline Village is a scenic mountain town that has recently attracted some of the world’s wealthiest, earning it the nickname “Income Village,” as billionaires including Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison and Google co-founder Sergey Brin have reportedly purchased homes in the area.

title: Trump signs order attempting to override CDC vaccine schedule and break up MMR shots
summary: President and RFK Jr, the health secretary, repeatedly referred to autism during signing, though studies show no link between it and vaccines
body: Donald Trump has signed an executive order with plans for sweeping changes to the childhood vaccination schedule that attempts to override the authority of the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC). It is an attempt to undergird the changes made earlier this year to CDC vaccination recommendations, which were halted by a federal judge. The CDC is the federal agency tasked with recommending vaccines, not the White House. The order would also require that the measles, mumps and rubella vaccine be broken into three separate shots, once it becomes available in the US. And it would recommend that all shots be given at separate medical visits, a frequent point Trump has made despite the safety, ease and lower costs of giving vaccines together. Only six of the 17 vaccines routinely recommended for all children in the US would continue to have full recommendations: measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), diphtheria, tetanus, pertussis (DTaP), polio, Hib, pneumococcal disease, HPV and varicella. “Together, there could be a possibility they’re quite lethal,” Trump said of the MMR vaccine at the signing of the order on Monday. Five other shots would be recommended only for those at high risk: monoclonal antibodies to protect against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV) as well as vaccines against hepatitis A, hepatitis B and meningococcal ACWY, which is currently recommended for teens and high-risk infants. Dengue and meningococcal B vaccines are also on this list, but dengue was already recommended only for those at risk and meningococcal B was shared clinical decision-making. And six shots would be pushed to shared clinical decision-making: hepatitis A, hepatitis B, rotavirus, meningococcal disease, influenza and Covid-19. This is a previously obscure category that means a provider would be required to weigh the risks and benefits, despite strong evidence for the safety and efficacy of these vaccines. The executive order would also require the MMR vaccine to be broken into three separate shots, which is not currently possible in the US as there are no separately licensed vaccines for measles, mumps and rubella and the licensing process takes years. The order also states that, “to the maximum extent feasible, all childhood immunizations should be administered at separate medical visits”. This would put a financial and logistical strain on families and medical providers by creating several additional visits. The US attorney general would also be tasked with challenging state laws that conflict with the executive order. The US has no vaccination mandates. Shots that are required for school attendance are set at the state and local level. Both Trump and Robert F Kennedy, the health secretary, made repeated mentions of autism throughout the order signing, emphasizing a scientifically unproven link between vaccines and the condition. Dozens of studies show no link between the two. “Today we’re proud to officially announce the United States of America’s gold standard childhood vaccination recommendations. That has to do with many subjects including autism in particular,” Trump said at the beginning of the order signing. “I’ve seen proof of it, where they have a vaccination where it looks like the size of a bottle of soda, poured into a little child’s body and bad things happen in too many cases,” Trump later said on breaking up each shot into an individual medical visit, before adding: “This is an explosion, it’s an epidemic,” in an apparent reference to autism. Kennedy claimed at one point: “Something happened in the mid-90s that changed our children, and it has to be an environmental exposure.” Rebuking these claims and ties to autism, Bill Cassidy, a Louisiana senator, tweeted in response to the order that it “is so wrong”. “I’m a doctor. This executive order is wrong. The President does not have the expertise to make these changes. Vaccines are overwhelmingly safe. Vaccines are effective. Vaccines DO NOT cause autism. Breaking up vaccines will mean children have to get more shots to get the same protection, not fewer shots. It will increase hesitancy and make children less safe. Parents should listen to their child’s pediatrician about vaccines rather than listening to an inaccurate executive order. This is so wrong,” Cassidy wrote. Executive orders are meant as guidance to federal agencies; they are not laws passed by Congress, and thus they have no legal effect on the public. “This should have no direct operational effects,” says Dorit Reiss, a vaccines expert at UC Law San Francisco. Twenty-nine states and the District of Columbia have decoupled their vaccination requirements from the CDC, and insurance continues to cover the shots. However, “Trump has influence,” Reiss said, and the order may intensify “political pressure on states” to change school requirements.

title: Trump demands Iran pay compensation for decades of US soldier deaths
summary: US president’s statement is latest sign that negotations to end war and reopen strait of Hormuz have stalled
body: Donald Trump has said he will demand that Iran pay compensation for the deaths of thousands of US soldiers and Iran’s own civilians killed in recent decades in the latest sign his negotiations to end the war and reopen the strait of Hormuz have reached an impasse. The US president is trying to end conflicts in Iran, Gaza and Lebanon, and his additional demands of Iran are likely to provoke anger in Tehran at the same time as Israel has rejected Trump’s terms for a 15-point roadmap to end the war in Gaza. In a post on Truth Social, Trump said he was issuing the demand for war reparations in response to Iranian negotiators making similar claims for damages for the five-month war that has killed thousands and devastated Iran’s military and economy. “Now I am likewise demanding compensation from Iran, for all of the people that they have killed and gravely wounded with their roadside bombs and many conflicts, for which they are famous, as led initially by Gen Soleimani, including the families of those killed on the USS Cole, and thousands of others killed in combat,” he wrote on Truth Social. “Additionally, compensation should be paid to the families of the hundreds of thousands of innocent protesters that Iran has killed over the last 50 years, not to mention the 52,000 that have been killed in the last five months.” The demands are likely to be a nonstarter for Iran’s leaders in the careful peace negotiations aimed at reopening the strait of Hormuz, through which 20% of global oil trade flowed before the US and Israel launched joint strikes on Iran in late February. Trump and other senior negotiators have claimed many times that a deal is imminent, although none has materialised. The remarks followed a series of setbacks for Trump’s efforts to end several Middle East conflicts before the midterm elections in November, in which high oil prices and inflation will probably hurt fellow Republicans at the polls. On Sunday, the Israeli prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, said he rejected the Trump-backed Board of Peace’s 15-point plan to end Israel’s war in Gaza. Netanyahu had said Hamas must fully disarm before Israel would consider pulling out of Gaza, rather than the phased withdrawal proposed by the Board of Peace. Netanyahu framed the decision as a rejection of US pressure on Israel to make peace in several wars in the Middle East. “Unlike all those who lecture us, we do what needs to be done for Israel’s security, and we can and know how to stand our ground, even against our best friends when necessary,” Netanyahu said. Trump has not replied to Netanyahu’s statement, which was a remarkably public break between the leaders of the US and its closest ally in the Middle East. But in response to a shouted question in the Oval Office on Monday, he said his relationship with Netanyahu was “very good”. Trump has sought to increase pressure on Iran. An hour after his first post demanding war reparations from Tehran, he broadened their scope to include the victims of recent wars throughout the region. “Also, with respect to the Iran negotiations, Iran should be responsible for the damages and death caused to the people of Lebanon, Syria, Yemen, and Gaza!” he wrote.

title: Todd Blanche, Trump’s former personal lawyer, sworn in as US attorney general
summary: Loyalist sworn in after Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation on Saturday morning
body: Todd Blanche has been sworn as US attorney general, cementing Donald Trump’s installation of his former personal attorney in charge of the Department of Justice. Blanche, who has been serving as acting attorney general since April, was confirmed in his new position during a ceremony at the White House on Monday. The 52-year-old is the second Senate-confirmed attorney general of Trump’s second term, after Pam Bondi, who was ousted earlier this year. He previously served as Trump’s personal criminal defense lawyer, representing him in the New York hush-money case and other criminal matters, before joining the administration as deputy attorney general in early 2025. “Congratulations to a great lawyer and an even better man!!!” the press secretary, Karoline Leavitt, posted on social media following his closed-door confirmation. Since taking over, Blanche has presided over the departure of more than 200 prosecutors and agents who worked on Trump-related investigations, pushed expansive theories of presidential power and suffered a string of courtroom setbacks, including a stinging ruling in which a federal judge sent her findings to bar authorities considering disciplinary action against him. He now officially takes over the department after Trump ousted his predecessor, Pam Bondi, who the president had become frustrated with over insufficient action from the Department of Justice against his political foes. Bondi’s tenure had also been dogged by controversy over the botched handling of the Jeffrey Epstein files, which still shadows the department, with lawmakers continuing to press for the full release of records and Democrats accusing Blanche of following Bondi’s playbook of stonewalling survivors and Congress alike. The Senate voted narrowly in favor of his confirmation in the role, with the Republican-led upper chamber voting 50-49 in the early hours of Saturday morning. Every Democrat rejected his nomination, as well as the Republican senators Susan Collins of Maine and Lisa Murkowski of Alaska.

title: July was hottest month ever recorded in US as heatwaves scorched country
summary: Scientists have made clear that the elevated heat in the US was being amplified by the human-caused climate crisis
body: July was the hottest month ever recorded in the US, with repeated, scorching heatwaves across much of the country helping shatter all previous monthly temperature records stretching back over the full 132 years of reliable measurements. Last month’s average temperature was 3.3F (1.8C) higher than the 20th century average for the contiguous United States, which excludes Alaska and Hawaii, according to new data from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (Noaa). This means the month was the hottest July, and hottest of all months, in records that go back to 1895. It surpasses previous high marks set in July 1936, in the teeth of Dust Bowl conditions, and July 2012. In July, the US blistered under three separate heat dome events, where soaring temperatures where held in place over a region by slow-moving high pressure weather systems. Extreme heat hit much of the US west, the Rockies, upper midwest, the Gulf of Mexico coast and south-east, according to Noaa. Wyoming recorded its hottest ever July amid temperatures a huge 5.1F above average. Parts of the US spent the month blanketed under a haze of wildfire smoke, with large blazes engulfing forests in Canada and the US’s Pacific north-west. Scientists have made clear that the elevated heat, along with vast fires, was being significantly amplified by the human-caused climate crisis, accelerated by the burning of fossil fuels. Heat-trapping gases released by the combustion of coal, oil and gas are driving up global temperatures and fueling deadly heatwaves that have this year roiled the US and Europe, which is having its hottest summer on record. Sprawling forest fires, resulting in the evacuations of hundreds of thousands of people and the inhalation of toxic smoke for millions more, have become a feature of the season in North America and Europe. The average monthly heat record set in July – although the record for maximum daily temperatures remains July 2024 – has taken a toll on the lives of many Americans, polling released by AP-NORC last week showed. Nearly half of people in the US said the impact on their electricity bills, which have risen even as people have sought to cool themselves with air conditioning, has been “major”. Meanwhile, about 40% of people said the heat had altered their travel plans. About two-thirds of people polled reported having their families’ outdoor activities affected by the extreme heat, while about half said their exercise routine had been hampered. The impacts across various areas of Americans’ lives are more widespread than when the same questions were asked two years ago, the polling found. Despite the unfolding consequences of the climate crisis, Donald Trump has continued his attempts to axe cheap clean energy and bolster the production of fossil fuels. The US president has called climate science “bullshit” and a “con job” in the past and has sought to encourage other countries to also burn more of the fossil fuels that are driving up temperatures beyond those which humans have ever lived in before. An unusually strong El Niño event, a periodic climate feature where a section of the Pacific Ocean heats up causing weather around the world to alter, is likely to cause next year to be the hottest on record globally, surpassing a record set just in 2024. Some scientists think the developing El Niño could even ensure that this year is the one that breaks the record. “The bottom line, though, is that we expect to set record global temperatures as long as carbon emissions continue to warm the planet, and typically these records are set during major El Niño events,” said Michael Mann, a climate scientist at the University of Pennsylvania.

title: Scores dead after powerful earthquake strikes western Colombia
summary: Quake of 7.4 magnitude collapses and severely damages buildings in several major cities, including Cali and Pereira
body: More than 100 people have died after a powerful earthquake struck western Colombia, collapsing and severely damaging scores of buildings in major cities including Cali and Pereira. The US and Colombian geological surveys reported that a 7.4-magnitude earthquake struck at 7.34am local time (13.34 BST) on Monday, with its epicentre in the western department of Chocó. It was also felt in neighbouring Venezuela, which is still reeling from a deadly double earthquake on 24 June. Colombia’s president, Abelardo de la Espriella, said 111 people had been killed and 87 injured, while 61 buildings had collapsed. “The ⁠national government has all of its capabilities deployed to protect lives, assist affected communities and deliver aid wherever it is needed,” he said in a national address at about 1pm local time, upon declaring ‌a national state of emergency. “The first priority is rescuing the people trapped under the rubble.” Western Colombia appears to have suffered the most serious damage, where authorities reported 27 deaths in the Valle del Cauca department, 40 deaths in Pereira, the capital of Risaralda department, and at least two in Manizales, the capital of Caldas. The mayor of Manizales, Jorge Eduardo Rojas Giraldo, said at least 12 buildings and 20 homes had been partially or completely or destroyed there. In a social media video, he told citizens to be “completely ready” for aftershocks. “Do not go back into the buildings yet. I know this isn’t easy but stay outside for a little while at least because there could be an aftershock,” he said. Social media videos showed citizens searching for victims in the wreckage of a four-storey hotel in Cali and a woman sprinting from a building as it collapsed in Manizales. One video showed part of San José church in Pereira collapsing as palm trees around it shook. Another video published by the newspaper El Tiempo captured the moment a building gave way in Manizales. The mayor of Cali, Alejandro Eder, said at least 20 buildings had collapsed in his city and that some people were trapped inside. He did not specify how many. “Right now, we are trying to map out what has happened, firstly to protect lives and secondly to be able to push ahead with any kind of rescue that might be necessary,” he said, urging citizens to stay calm. He also told residents to check their buildings for structural damage. “If you do not feel safe, if you see very large cracks, please leave the building,” he said. The mayor of Pereira, Mauricio Salazar, declared a curfew. In an interview with local radio he said 65 buildings had collapsed, with victims thought to be trapped in at least 15 of them. Five of the city’s hospitals were reportedly inundated with the injured. Raúl Andrés Buitrago, the head of customer service at a business in Pereira, described setting off for work when the seismic alert on his watch went off. “There are often little tremors here,” he said. “But I’d never felt an earthquake like this. It started softly, softly, softly, then it felt like it was getting stronger every second.” He spoke of “horrible” scenes as he fled outside on to the street in the city centre, which is home to many old buildings. “The roofs started to fall in. The buildings collapsed in on themselves. The panic was terrible. They were the four longest minutes of my life,” he said. The governor of Chocó, Nubia Carolina Córdoba, said people had been injured and buildings severely damaged in the department’s capital, Quibdó. De la Espriella, who took office on Friday, flew to the capital, Bogotá, where he said he would lead the government response. “Colombia has a president whose heart aches for his people and who will do everything in his power to help them in the most difficult moments,” he said in a video posted on his official social networks. His office announced that he had ordered an immediate meeting of the national disaster management committee and said the government was “vigilant and in action”. “We will keep Colombians informed,” it said. Aviation authorities said the airports in Pereira, Manizales, Quibdó, Cartago, Armenia and Buenaventura had sustained damage. The earthquake comes weeks after Venezuela was struck by twin earthquakes that devastated the country’s northern coast, killing more than 6,000 people. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, said the Trump administration – which has thrown its weight behind Colombia’s new rightwing president – was monitoring the situation closely and stood ready to offer its support.

title: Labour peer urges Tories to sack former neo-Nazi who abused her
summary: Badenoch adviser Joshua Bonehill-Paine was found guilty in 2016 of racially aggravated harassment of then MP Luciana Berger
body: The Labour peer Luciana Berger has urged Kemi Badenoch to “listen to victims” and reverse her decision to give a national advisory role to a former neo-Nazi. Joshua Bonehill-Paine was jailed in 2015 for more than three years after posting antisemitic material online before a planned neo-Nazi rally. In 2016, he was found guilty of racially aggravated harassment for abuse directed at Berger, an MP at the time. He was also the founder and leader of the National British Resistance, a far-right group. Berger said she was still affected by his crimes more than nine years later, and questioned what safeguarding checks Badenoch and the Conservative party had carried out in relation to his appointment to the party’s culture and integration commission. Berger, who is Jewish, asked whether Bonehill-Paine’s new role could bring him to Westminster. She wrote on X: “Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate?” Badenoch’s spokesperson said Bonehill-Paine would not have a parliamentary pass and would not be on the estate. Berger’s intervention came after the Conservative party leader published a lengthy defence of Bonehill-Paine in the Times, describing questions over his suitability to stand as a councillor in Somerset as a “pile-on”. Bonehill-Paine was set to stand as a Tory local councillor but announced last week that he had withdrawn from next year’s local elections after Badenoch offered him the advisory role. Badenoch said: “People need to understand that the Conservative party under my leadership is now the party of personal responsibility and law and order. That means insisting on consequences by punishing wrongdoing and protecting the public, especially victims. “We need fewer double standards and instead higher standards in a system that is repeatedly failing to protect the public. We should be tough enough to stand by our beliefs even when politically inconvenient, wise enough to recognise rehabilitation and consistent enough to apply the same principles to friend and foe.” Berger said she had seen the piece late on Saturday night and “tried to ignore it” but after Badenoch shared the article on Monday, the former MP for Liverpool Wavertree accused her of giving insufficient consideration to Bonehill-Paine’s victims. “Badenoch makes one passing reference to the ‘victims’,” Berger wrote. “There were many. And I was one of them. Did Badenoch read the judge’s sentencing remarks? In court we heard the victim impact statements from people unable to testify, whose lives he had destroyed. “His appointment as an adviser to the Conservative party’s culture and integration commission could conceivably bring him to Westminster. Can I expect to come face to face with him on the parliamentary estate? “It’s still not too late for Badenoch to listen to victims and reverse her decision.” A spokesperson for Badenoch said Bonehill-Paine had served his time, completed Home Office Prevent (counter-terrorism) courses, and had gone into schools to teach about combatting antisemitism and extremism. But the party did not answer questions about what safeguarding checks it had carried out in relation to his appointment as an adviser, or why Badenoch had not contacted Berger. The abuse Bonehill-Paine directed at Berger included calling her a “rodent” and an “evil money-grabber”. He also has a conviction for assaulting a police officer and burglary of a police station, and was convicted in 2014 of malicious communications over an anti-Islam hoax that led to death threats against the owners of a pub in Leicester. Berger challenged Badenoch over what consideration had been given to safeguarding: “Badenoch’s article says she wants to safeguard the public and victims, but what safeguarding checks have she and the Conservative party carried out?” If Badenoch or her team had reached out to her, Berger said, “I would say, I don’t think it is ‘harder politics’ for this man to be part of Kemi’s operation. I think it’s the wrong politics.” She added: “I’m all for rehabilitation. But someone convicted of neo-Nazi misogynistic crimes is not suitable for public office less than a decade after his conviction. And neither should he be gifted a national advisory role, even closer to power.”

title: Water companies circumventing bonus rules? What did ministers expect?
summary: Door was left open to such behaviour because the regulator for England and Wales can only use the powers it was given by parliament
body: Anybody who followed the supposed “clampdown” on bankers’ bonuses after the great financial crash in 2008 knew what to expect when water company bosses became a similar target for a bash in the bonus department. We would see the waterbed principle in action: when you push down in one area of remuneration, such as the performance-related stuff, another tends to go up. Back in the day, banks invented “role-based allowances” – salary top-ups – to “compensate”, as they put it, their top earners for being subject to EU caps on bonuses. No executive was seriously inconvenienced by forgoing the chance of an astronomical (but not guaranteed) bonus and getting a smaller (but still hefty) increase in fixed pay instead. Some even preferred greater certainty over what they would take home. In water-land, the Labour government arrived in 2024 promising to “ban the payment of bonuses to polluting water bosses until they have cleaned up their filth”, which generated a few pleasing headlines. But the flaw in the resulting Water (Special Measures) Act 2025 was obvious. While the regulator for England and Wales, Ofwat, was given powers to block performance-related bonuses at the worst environmental and financial miscreants, it could do nothing formally about other payments. Thus – surprise, surprise – salary increases, allowance awards and, most of all, retention payments have proliferated. After the English and Welsh companies published their annual reports last month, this newspaper found that overall reported pay packets rose by 1.5% to £25.3m for chief executives and chief financial officers for the year. It was the second year in a row that a bonus ban had resulted in higher overall pay across the sector. One can usually rely on Thames Water to muddy things further, and its post-annual report contribution was the news that the chief financial officer, Steve Buck, who was paid £591,000 in the financial year to March, got a delayed £1m signing fee at the end of July. As for retention payments for other executives that were “paused” after a political kerfuffle a year ago, the company has “entered into 14 agreements” to “resolve its liability for any potential claims”. The government is shocked, or pretends to be. “It is unacceptable that one of the worst-performing water companies is handing out huge payments to its executives when it should be focusing on improving performance and rebuilding public trust,” a spokesperson for the environment department said. Again, though, one must ask: what did ministers think would happen? It’s easy to agree that executives of underperforming monopolies are grossly overpaid but it was fantastically naive on the part of politicians to think a ban on bonuses would not result in alternative wheezes. It was predictable. Water companies in general have deployed the retention manoeuvre in less-than-transparent – or just shameless – ways, it should be added. Helen Campbell, the interim executive director of Ofwat, was clearly correct last month when she complained that customers’ trust is harmed when remuneration committees make decisions that “give the appearance of circumventing the rule” or aren’t explained. The point, though, is that the government left the door wide open to such behaviour. If ministers were relying on remuneration committees to obey the “spirit” of their reforms, they were born yesterday. Restricting bonuses is not the same as restricting overall pay. And Ofwat can use only the powers it was given by parliament. The dance now moves to the regulator’s review, due in the autumn, of whether the rules should be strengthened. Maybe it will yield something different in the prime minister Andy Burnham’s undefined era of “greater public control”. On past experience, however, believe it when you see it.

title: Flip-flopping Netanyahu rejects Gaza plan but cannot placate all his allies
summary: Israeli prime minister faces incompatible demands from his far-right government ministers and from Donald Trump
body: Benjamin Netanyahu’s public rejection of a US-backed deal for Gaza drew scepticism in Israel, amid reports he was personally hammering out details of a pilot military withdrawal days earlier. The Israeli prime minister is struggling to balance incompatible demands on Gaza policy from his key domestic and international allies. The far-right Israeli politicians who prop up Netanyahu’s coalition government want to intensify Israeli attacks on Gaza and establish settlements inside the territory. Donald Trump, who provides vital diplomatic and military backing for Israel, wants to move toward a permanent settlement and return to Palestinian control in Gaza, brokered by the Board of Peace that he created and chairs. With an Israeli election looming in just over two months, Netanyahu appears to have opted to publicly placate domestic partners who are already on the campaign trail. On Sunday, he rejected a new 15-point plan for Gaza, which included a Hamas commitment to give up its weapons, meeting a key Israeli demand. He also resisted US pressure to end wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran without Israel’s buy-in. The remarks blindsided Israeli commanders, who had been discussing the implementation of the plan in meetings with Netanyahu and the IDF’s chief of staff, Eyal Zamir, days earlier, Israel’s Channel 12 television reported. “We learned about it today from the media,” the station quoted a defence official as saying. “At the meetings that were held until now, the prime minister personally gave his consent to this plan and to a withdrawal from the points in Rafah.” The meetings covered precise boundaries of three pilot areas in southern Gaza where a proposed international force – which has yet to be stood up – could take over from the Israeli military, and the interface between the two forces, the report said. Netanyahu’s public attack on the Board of Peace plan seemed like a particularly pointed rejection of US goals because it was released soon after a reported visit by Adm Brad Cooper, who heads US Central Command. He came to deliver in person the message that the Trump administration wants Israel to end its wars in Gaza and Lebanon, Israeli media reported. “The Americans’ message to the IDF was to move in the direction of shutting down all three theatres of operations,” a senior Israeli military officer told Channel 13 Television. Defying Trump, who is notoriously thin-skinned and intolerant of dissent, is risky when Israel is internationally isolated and needs US military supplies. But Netanyahu has a long track record of audacious political manoeuvring, both at home and internationally, undaunted even by ostensible power imbalances. Bill Clinton, after meeting him for the first time in 1996, is reported to have said: “Who’s the fucking superpower here?” In May 2024, the then US president, Joe Biden, announced an Israeli-backed ceasefire and hostage release plan for Gaza, only to have Netanyahu distance himself from the proposal and ultimately reject it. For now the administration in Washington appears to have largely shrugged off Netanyahu’s comments as electioneering, perhaps encouraged by military decisions that indicate a far more attentive regard for Trump’s wishes. Last week, Netanyahu scaled back Israeli airstrikes on Gaza by raising the threshold for authorising attacks. Targeted killings must now be approved by the chief of staff, rather than the regional commander, unless Israeli forces are in “imminent danger”. Nor is this the first time he has bowed to US pressure to rein in wars that have the enthusiastic backing of his far-right allies, recently limiting the offensive in Lebanon, and last year ordering fighter jets heading for Iran to turn back at Trump’s demand. Netanyahu’s combination of fierce domestic rhetoric and some conciliatory steps on the ground in Gaza may have bought him a bit of time but US patience may not last until polling day in late October. Trump is weighing up election concerns of his own, as the US is holding midterms just a week after Israel votes. Netanyahu’s visit to the White House last month was notably low profile for a leader who has repeatedly campaigned on his reputation as an international statesman and close relationship with the US president, Haaretz newspaper noted. It ended without a joint statement, and strains caused by the Israeli prime minister’s competing political priorities have become increasingly evident. “That’s how it is when you try to juggle too many balls; you start dropping them,” the paper said. The top envoy for the Board of Peace, Nickolay Mladenov, declined to comment on Netanyahu’s rejection of a deal that took months to hammer out. In an interview with Israeli media he said only that “discussions continue”. Palestinians in Gaza have endured nearly a year of deadly limbo after Trump brokered a nominal ceasefire last October, that he said would halt fighting and pave the way for reconstruction. Israeli attacks have continued, killing over 1,200 people, and Israel has blocked the entry of equipment, supplies and fuel needed for rebuilding homes, schools and medical infrastructure. The majority of Gaza’s surviving population live in tent camps with little sanitation, and although hunger has diminished food shortages are still widespread, with over 70,000 children projected to need treatment for acute malnutrition to April 2027, food security experts have warned. Netanyahu’s office rejected reports that he had discussed detailed withdrawal plans for Gaza.

title: Police use teargas on young Indians as government jobs protest escalates
summary: Demonstrators accuse authorities of failing to tackle irregularities in exams for sought-after civil service jobs
body: Thousands of angry young job-seekers clashed with police in Jharkhand, one of India’s poorest states, on Monday as a weeks-long protest over alleged irregularities in recruitment drives for coveted government jobs escalated into a march on the state legislature. Police fired water cannon and teargas and swung batons as they tried to stop flag-waving demonstrators from clambering over barricades and surging towards the assembly in Ranchi, the state capital. Some of the protesters responded by dancing and cheering as jets of water drenched the crowd. The unrest comes just weeks after the Cockroach movement, a youth-led protest campaign – which began as an online joke and grew into a nationwide outcry over leaks in a national medical entrance examination – put the BJP-led national government under heavy pressure and led to the resignation of the education minister. Both protesters and police officers were injured in the Jharkhand clashes, local media reported, although no official figures were released. “The baton charge was barbaric. We were protesting peacefully, but the government used batons against us,” protester Piyush Kumar Soni told the Press Trust of India. The demonstrators are demanding an investigation by the CBI, India’s premier investigative force, saying only an independent inquiry can get to the bottom of alleged wrongdoing in government recruitment examinations. They accuse authorities of failing to prevent irregularities in public service exams, including test paper leaks and cheating, and say the alleged scandals have deprived young people of a fair chance. Jharkhand has long struggled with high unemployment, making government jobs highly sought after. Competition is intense for civil service and other public sector posts, which offer job security, health and pension benefits. Government recruitment drives routinely attract hundreds of thousands of applicants, and many young people spend years preparing for examinations. In one recent Jharkhand recruitment exercise, nearly 640,000 applications were received for 2,025 posts. In another, more than 322,000 candidates competed for 510 vacancies. The state government, led by a regional party allied with the opposition Congress, has sought to defuse the crisis through talks. Officials say most of the protesters’ demands have been accepted and that they are open to more negotiations. The Congress leader, Rahul Gandhi, condemned the use of force. “Students have a right to peaceful protest, and only dialogue can yield solutions,” he said. The row has already toppled senior figures. The former Jharkhand public service commission chair was arrested over alleged exam irregularities, while three commission members have resigned. The protests underscore mounting frustration among young Indians over corruption in public examinations and recruitment systems, a shortage of good jobs and fears that opportunities are being lost to cheating and political influence. Nearly two-thirds of Indians are under 35. Official data shows unemployment fell to 9.9% last year, but a 2026 study by Azim Premji University found that nearly 40% of graduates aged 15 to 25 were unemployed.

title: Ukraine drone strike on oil refinery deep inside Russia kills at least 13
summary: Attack hundreds of miles from border would be among deadliest of war as Kyiv aims to strangle Russian economy
body: A Ukrainian drone strike on an industrial city deep inside Russia has killed at least 13 people, according to the local mayor, as Kyiv steps up its campaign of long-range strikes on targets far from the frontline. Kyiv said it hit the Taneco refinery in the city of Nizhnekamsk, about 750 miles (1,200km) from the Ukrainian border. Footage circulating online appeared to show smoke rising from the refinery. Ukraine’s general staff said the raid was part of a campaign to reduce the “military potential of the Russian aggressor”. Russian investigators claimed civilian and industrial sites in the city had been hit. The head of the Tatarstan region, Rustam Minnikhanov, said a Ukrainian drone hit a hostel, killing nine people. He posted images showing a badly damaged building. If the death toll is confirmed, the strike would be among the deadliest Ukrainian attacks on Russian territory since the full-scale invasion began in 2022, underscoring the growing reach of Kyiv’s strikes deep inside Russia. The Uzbek consulate said in a Telegram post that seven of the victims were Uzbek citizens. Minnikhanov declared a day of mourning and Russian prosecutors opened a criminal case into alleged terrorism. Local video footage showed Ukrainian drones buzzing above the city’s skyline, flying low over grey and box-like Soviet-era apartment blocks. Two plumes of black smoke could be seen rising above an industrial zone on the wooded outskirts of Nizhnekamsk. The site is home to Taneco, one of Russia’s biggest and most technologically advanced oil refineries, owned by Tatneft. It also houses a plant that produces rubber and petrochemical products. Ukraine also bombed the area in June. In an address on Sunday, Volodymyr Zelenskyy said “long-range sanctions” against the Kremlin and its war machine would continue. In recent months Ukrainian drones have wreaked havoc on Russia’s oil export industry, even hitting refineries in Siberia, 1,500 miles from the frontline. The governor of the Tyumen region in western Siberia said on Monday that several Ukrainian drones had fallen on an industrial facility and that emergency services were dealing with a fire. There have been several strikes on warehouses belonging to Wildberries, Russia’s equivalent of Amazon, as well as on oil tankers in the Sea of Azov and Black Sea. Ukraine’s long-term goal is to slowly strangle the Russian economy so Moscow can no longer fund its war. Zelenskyy described his country’s remote bombing campaign as “entirely justified”. “Every Russian strike [on Ukrainian towns and cities] will be met with our response. Russia’s war will be felt more and more at their own home – in Russia,” he said on social media. “The only reason this is still continuing is Russia’s unwillingness to end this war.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had intercepted 456 Ukrainian drones flying above Russian territory and annexed Crimea. Ukraine says it is knocking out its opponent’s air defence systems more quickly than they can be replaced, creating air corridors or “doors” it can exploit. Overnight, Ukraine’s armed forces hit equipment depots and a repair unit in the occupied Donetsk and Luhansk parts of eastern Ukraine, while ⁠Russian-appointed local authorities said the ⁠Zaporizhzhia region in south-east Ukraine was largely without ⁠electricity on Monday ⁠after Ukrainian attacks destroyed key power facilities. On Russia’s Black Sea ⁠coast, power outages were reported in ‌parts of ‌Novorossiysk, a major export ‌port, and in the holiday resort of Gelendzhik, regional authorities said on Telegram. There were unconfirmed reports that Russian ballistic missile launcher systems were destroyed inside Russia, not far from the border. According to Telegram channels citing Ukrainian military sources, the targeted high-value military assets were in Russia’s western Kursk and Bryansk regions. Both were used to launch Iskander and hypersonic Zircon missiles towards Kyiv. Ukrainian prosecutors said five people were killed on Sunday in a Russian artillery strike on a village outside Kharkiv. Several houses were flattened as a result of an “enemy strike” on Buhaivka in the Chuhuiv district, they said. Sweden’s security service, Säpo, said on Monday it ⁠had shut down a Russian spying operation that had tried to ⁠influence decision making ⁠there and discredit the Nordic country as well as its EU and ⁠Nato allies. Säpo said the operation had been planned and directed by Russia’s SVR foreign ⁠intelligence service and involved three people working under the cover of ‌diplomatic immunity. “This is ‌consistent with the threat we see Russia posing,” a Säpo spokesperson said. “We have been able to monitor what happened at these meetings between the individuals involved, what was said and what assignments were given. They are ⁠no longer in Sweden and we have been able to break up this operation.”

title: Amnesty International says Farage putting ‘hate and inhumanity’ over leadership with El Salvador prison plan – as it happened
summary: A spokesperson for the human rights group likened the proposal to ‘financial brutality with British taxpayers’ money’
body: Andy Burnham has been warned that changing the terms of the prisoners’ early release scheme so PC Andrew Harper’s killers are kept behind bars would force another spate of early releases before the next general election. A dinghy carrying a record 230 people has arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel in the early hours of Monday. Amnesty International UK has condemned Reform UK’s proposal to send foreign prisoners to serve the rest of their sentences in El Salvador, saying it is an example of politicians choosing to put “hate, violence and inhumanity” ahead of leadership. (See 2.23pm.) GB News is being investigated by the UK’s media regulator after a guest appeared to link pride parades with bestiality and paedophilia. The Treasury “materially contributed” to the death of Chloe Moffat, a 26-year-old personal assistant who took her own life after facing disciplinary proceedings, a coroner has found. For a full list of all the stories covered on the blog today, do scroll through the list of key event headlines near the top of the blog. Danny Shaw, the home affairs commentator and former BBC correspondent who briefly worked as a Labour adviser on home affairs policy, says he thinks Downing Street is wrong to say it can’t find a way of excluding PC Andrew Harper’s killers from the early release scheme. (See 12.46pm.) This is wrong. Govt can block Pc Harper’s killers’ early release and ensure there’s enough prison space - through emergency legislation in September: 1. Exclude prisoners jailed for 10+ years for manslaughter from early release (220 people, including Pc Harper’s killers, Bowers and Cole) 2. Release on tag & curfew, after risk assessment, people jailed for up to 12 months (up to 2,700 people). All it takes is imagination and political will. Reform UK has confirmed that it would legislate to stop charities helping asylum seekers who come to the UK. Responding to an Express report about how many items Care4Calais has given to help migrants in France and the UK, Zia Yusuf, Reform’s home affairs spokesperson, said: Care4Calais is not a charity. It is a facilitator of illegal migration, actively aiding the mass arrival of unvetted, fighting-age males into Britain at a cost of billions to the taxpayer. Successive Tory and Labour governments have colluded by looking the other way. Reform UK will pass the ‘Polanski Law’ to criminalise any act that assists or encourages illegal entry, punishable by two years’ imprisonment. We will treat those who enable this invasion as the accomplices they are and shut them down immediately. Yusuf described this as “Polanski’s law” when he first proposed it earlier this year because Zack Polanski, the Green party leader, is a proud supporter of the rights of asylum seekers. The Scottish Conservatives are urging the Scottish Greens to withdraw the whip from the MSP’s comment about rape being a “spectrum”. (See 1.48pm.) Meghan Gallacher, equalities spokesperson for the Scottish Tories, said: These remarks from an extremist Scottish Greens MSP were appalling and beyond the pale. It is deeply alarming that anyone, but especially an elected representative, would ever seek to minimise the seriousness of rape and suggest that there is a spectrum of offences. Q Manivannan’s comments were so unacceptable that I believe Scottish Greens co-leaders Ross Greer and Gillian Mackay must now remove the whip from them. Aileen O’Connor, chair of the Thames Valley Police Federation, has said that Downing Street’s failure to block the early release of two of the men who killed PC Andrew Harper (see 12.46pm) is “indefensible”. In a statement, she said: The public are speaking loudly and clearly. They agree with us that the government are firmly on the wrong side of this. What they are doing is indefensible. And they simply cannot defend it. They must listen. The prime minister must listen. If you kill a police officer there should be no early release. No ifs. No buts. Haroon Siddique has a good explainer on the options available to the PM. Thames Water has paid its finance chief a £1m signing fee despite teetering on the brink of a government-handled administration, in a decision which the environment department labelled “unacceptable”. Jasper Jolly has the story. Chris Philp, the shadow home secretary, has claimed that the arrival of a boat carrying 230 migrants shows the French are not trying to tackle the problem. In a statement he said: This is now beyond a joke. The French authorities could easily have stopped a vessel this size from embarking in shallow waters. I recently saw for myself French Gendarmes standing by and doing nothing while illegal immigrants boarded in knee deep water. Shabana Mahmood [the home secretary] is handing over £660m of our money while this happens. It’s a disgrace. Ipsos UK has released some polling today suggesting Labour now has a 3-point lead over Reform UK. This is Labour’s best result in an Ipsos poll for more than a year. But, although Andy Burnham’s arrival as PM has given Labour a boost, only two prime ministers since 1979 have taken office with satisfaction with the government at a lower level. They were Boris Johnson in 2019 and Rishi Sunak in 2022. And only three former PMs since 1979 have had lower personal approval ratings at this point than Burnham’s are now. They were Johnson, Sunak and Liz Truss. Commenting on the findings, Gideon Skinner, senior director of politics at Ipsos UK, said: These findings confirm Labour are benefiting from changing their leader, with their best position in Ipsos polling for over a year. However, while Andy Burnham is clearly much more personally liked than his predecessor was at the end of his term (and more than the opposition party leaders, who typically the public don’t yet see as ready to replace him), at the moment his position can be seen as part benefit of the doubt and part jury is still out. Although Labour has received a boost in voting intentions (partly thanks to more of their 2024 base returning to the fold), many of the underlying issues remain. The Labour party itself is still less liked than it has been for most of the last 20 years, and 7 in 10 are still dissatisfied how the country is being run overall – the ongoing pessimism of recent times has dampened public enthusiasm that a new PM will be able to quickly turn around the direction of the country. Amnesty International UK has condemned Reform UK’s proposal to send foreign prisoners to serve the rest of their sentences in El Salvador. In a statement on the policy announced at a press conference this morning (see 9.35am), Steve Valdez-Symonds, Amnesty International UK’s refugee and migrant rights director, said: Reform is proposing to contract into serious human rights abuses in El Salvador to enable the transfer of people convicted in the UK into an extremely overcrowded and abusive prison system overseas – financing brutality with British taxpayers’ money. Amnesty has documented mass arbitrary detention, beatings, torture and other ill-treatment, enforced disappearances, denial of medical care and deaths in custody in El Salvador. People have been cut off from their families and effectively disappeared into detention, while relatives have been left searching prisons, courts and even morgues for answers. This proposal is a further extension of a wider politics that has moved dangerously far from any sense of what is practical, legal or constitutes basic human decency. We have already seen with the Rwanda scheme how policies once considered unthinkable can be pushed dangerously far when politicians choose headlines and hostility over real solutions to human needs. Too many politicians seem incapable of any real leadership – whether at home or internationally – preferring to agitate hate, violence and inhumanity that makes all of us less safe. This latest proposal from Reform provides a stark example of that. Downing Street says the arrival of a record 230 people in the UK on a single ‘mega-dinghy’ crossing the Channel has highlighted the “ruthless” tactics being used by people smugglers. Asked about the incident at the No 10 lobby briefing, the PM’s spokesperson said: We’ve seen today some appalling images of young babies being put into these unseaworthy craft, and they’re shocking images, and they show the reality behind the ruthless smuggling gangs that are prepared to risk human lives for profit. That’s exactly why the government has signed a new payment-by-results deal with the French to prevent these perilous journeys from happening in the first place. The government was “not complacent”, the spokesperson said. But he said joint action taken with the French since the general election had prevented 47,000 crossings. A dinghy carrying a record 230 people has arrived in the UK after crossing the Channel in the early hours of Monday, Diane Taylor reports. The Scottish Rape Crisis Alliance (SRCA) has condemned a Green MSP over their comments about the “demonisation of rape”, the Press Association reports. PA says: Q Manivannan was also rebuked for saying rape exists on a “spectrum”. Manivannan has faced backlash from Scotland’s children’s minister, as well as Labour, the Conservatives and the Liberal Democrats. The comments from Manivannan, made during The Subjective Space podcast last year, sparked fury after they re-emerged online at the weekend.
